ment has set forth its policy in regard to the future of our air lines, I am not so sure that any policy has been set forth as to the future of the aircraft industry, and this afternoon I want to ask the minister a few questions on that subject. I shall state all my questions while I am on my feet, and I hope the minister may be able to make a statement with regard to the policy of the government in this matter. First, what is to be our position after the war with regard to the acquisition of aeroplane engines? That matter has been discussed time and again during the last few years. I think the minister made it quite clear that it was not the policy of his department to embark, during war years, upon the manufacture of aeroplane engines in this country. He suggested, and I think perhaps rightly, that our war effort could be better facilitated by importing engines from countries that had much more experience in that field. The question arises, of course: are we to remain indefinitely in the position of being dependent upon other countries for the engines we will use in our commercial aviation? That is the first question I submit for the minister's consideration. The second question is: what will 6e our position in post-war days with regard to the production of transport planes? My information is that one-third of all the planes of the United States army and navy are transport planes, and that in the United States they have huge factories engaged in the production of these planes. On Tuesday evening the Minister of National Defence for Air indicated that Canada will be or is dependent upon the United States for transport planes to be used in training on our own fields, and that the government had received information that a number of these transport planes would be delivered by United States factories later this year. Are steps being taken to ensure that we can produce in Canada the type of plane that will be needed for heavy transport in the post-war years?
My third question is: what is to be our position in regard to the ownership of the aircraft industry, which at present is partly government-owned and partly privately-owned? The Progressive Conservative party, I assume, have announced their stand on this question; I should like to give my understanding of their position, and if I am wrong I am sure the leader of the opposition will correct me. Both the Premier of Ontario and the leader of the opposition, speaking in the Toronto district, voiced considerable protest over the placing of contracts for transport planes with the Vickers plant in Montreal instead of with the government-owned plant at Malton. I presume their protest was based upon the fact that a privately-owned company 
was getting that contract rather than a publicly-owned company, and that as a result the privately-owned plant would have a lead over the government-owned plant in post-war years. I am quite sure both these gentlemen are much too big and much too concerned with the national welfare to take a geographical or provincial point of view on that question. I am quite sure the basis of their criticism was not the fact that this business was being given to a city in a sister province rather than to a city in Ontario. As yet the government has not announced its policy; whether in the post-war years it will lend its support to the publicly-owned aircraft plants or to the privately-owned plants, or whether the one or the other or both are to be assisted in developing Canada's post-war civil aviation.
Another question is with regard to the government's policy concerning assistance in the post-war years to the aircraft industry, whether publicly or privately owned. As I have indicated, this industry has been built up over the years by the expenditure of public money; and I think it is generally agreed that if the aircraft industy in Canada is to compete with that of other, larger countries, regardless of whether it is publicly or privately owned, it will, in large measure, have to depend upon government support and assistance in order to meet that competition. It will need assistance, perhaps by way of subsidies or government contracts that will be assured for a given number of years, so that in the realm of manufacturing costs it may be able to compete with Great Britain and the United States.
Another question is: what type of plane is to be developed as most useful for the postwar period; upon what designs are we to concentrate? Has the government given any consideration to this question; has it reached any decision, or is that matter being investigated at the present time?
There is the further question of our position with regard to designing staffs capable of competing with similar staffs in other countries. I think it is generally agreed that if Canada is to maintain a successful aircraft industry in the post-war years, such designing staffs as we have at present should be retained in Canada, and in that industry. Unquestionably some government consideration and government support will be required to be given in that field.
Then there is the question of how such work as will be available in the aircraft industry after the war shall be distributed among the firms, both publicly and privately owned, which are now in that business. Decisions will have to be made as to which of those plants, or how many of them are to remain in the business in the post-war years.

Mr. Chairman, I am not at all sure that what I have in mind might properly be discussed now. However, it will be recalled that, after the last war, not only members of the armed forces but the civilian population in general were anxious to get away from anything and everything that savoured of war. In sharp contrast with that prevailing thought there were small groups in many centres of Canada who envisioned what air transport could mean to the development of this country. These small groups of individuals formed themselves into flying clubs. These flying clubs through the activities and energy and self-sacrifice of certain individuals have contributed a great deal in the way of money and otherwise to creating an air consciousness. They were primarily responsible for maintaining a semblance of air service in many parts of Canada and they provided facilities for the training of young men. These flying clubs promoted model aircraft leagues, made up of the youth of the country who were thus able to acquire skilled knowledge in con-
nection with amateur air construction and aeronautics. When Canada began to lay the foundations of an air force she drew heavily upon the personnel of these flying clubs.
These clubs grew to such proportions that they ultimately banded together into the dominion fljdng clubs association. I have been present on occasion when the minister and his worthy deputy, Commander Edwards, and other members of the Department of Transport have expressed their tribute in glowing terms of the work done by these flying clubs. When war broke out and the department established elementary flying schools, in many cases they turned to the flying clubs and asked them to manage the schools. This was done with conspicuous success as is evidenced by the repeated statements of the Minister of National Defence for Air and many members of his department.
Matters have progressed to the point where elementary training schools and air schools in various parts of Canada are being abandoned. In the building up of these schools there has been developed a group of individuals who are experienced in administration, while another group has obtained considerable skill and experience in the mechanics and repair of aeroplanes. A number of trained airmen have been employed in the last three or four years as instructors and as managers of elementary flying schools.
I do not wish to be narrow or provincial in my remarks, but I can best illustrate what I have in mind by referring to the Regina flying club which has managed No. 15 elementary flying school during the past four years. This is one of the schools that are to be abandoned. It has a civilian personnel of some 258 persons, who, as I have mentioned, have gained considerable experience and skill. I should like to know if in the development of civilian air operations there will be a place for the men who have gained this experience. Is there to be a place in future civilian operations for the flying clubs in recognition of what they have done for aviation during the last twenty or more years?
I wish to know if in the development of civilian aviation there is any immediate prospect of the development of routes in western Canada, either north or south of the main line of Trans-Canada Air Lines, which would provide opportunities for the individuals to whom I have just referred? We hear frequent rumours of the desire and inclination of certain United States lines to enter western Canada, in particular Northwest Air Lines which operates from Chicago and Minneapolis, through Regina to Edmonton and on into Alaska. Can the minister tell us of any

possible developments which would provide opportunities for the men to whom I have just referred? I know the minister will be glad, as he has been on previous occasions, to pay tribute to the excellent public service which members of the flying clubs throughout Canada have rendered to the development of civil aviation and the proud position which Canada occupies in the air picture.

I am very glad to endorse everything the hon. member for Regina has said about the flying clubs. These clubs rendered a great contribution to the development of aviation in Canada prior to the war, and have also performed great service in the advancement of the war effort by sponsoring elementary training at various airports across Canada. The Department of Transport has been a strong supporter of these flying clubs since their inception and an annual grant is still made to the flying clubs association. While the work for which the flying clubs were organized has been suspended, the usefulness of the clubs has not ended. In some cases the flying clubs which undertook responsibility for elementary training have finished their work, and it will be necessary for them to suspend training activities for the time being. Because of the necessity of saving gasoline, and for other reasons, it has been determined as a matter of policy that training activities, for the time being, shall be confined to the Royal Canadian Air Force, but the day will come when we shall be glad to have the flying clubs resume training in which they were engaged before the war.
My hon. friend has dealt with the activities of the men who supported the flying clubs. I suggest to him that the policy of the government in connection with the operation of feeder lines, may offer a field of activity for some of the men who supported the flying clubs prior to the war. It is our desire to have a number of small operations in civil aviation to supplement the Trans-Canada operation. It is our desire that the men coming back from overseas should be able to enter into civilian flying as owners rather than as employees; I suggest to the directors of our flying clubs that they could find a very useful field of activity in surveying routes that could be made self-supporting and in banding themselves together to sponsor that kind of civilian operation. I throw that out for what it is worth. My hon. friend asked the question, and I am giving him an offhand suggestion.

I would have spoken three hours ago had the hon. member who was then in the Chair adhered to his written and verbal promise. However, to proceed to the item under discussion, I should like to ask the minister three questions and they are all to the point. Is it the policy of the government to aid the formation of municipal air bases in the vicinity of towns? If so, to what extent? If, for instance, the site were provided free by the municipality, what contribution would the government be prepared to make?
Most of these claims put forward by private members centre around some particular case in their respective ridings, and it is no different in my own case. The situation I have in mind is this. The city of Port Alberni has requested me to bring forward its claim for assistance toward an aerodrome in the vicinity. The Alberni valley contains a population of something like 10,000 or 11,000 people, and Port Alberni is the largest centre in it. We are cut off from any of the air facilities, and it takes us a day to go to Vancouver where we can get such. Primarily we are looking forward to the use of this aerodrome in connection with the development of the town and there are ample evidences that such service will be increasingly required. The town is growing, not only from war development but by reason of certain industries recently located there, and while the most outstanding feature in our mind is the usefulness of this provision as developments occur

after the war, yet I have in my hand evidence that it would be useful to a certain extent [DOT]during the period of the war itself.
I will not give any names, because it might possibly be of interest to the enemy, but planes come from Vancouver and the east [DOT]coast over the Beaufort range to the west coast to certain air bases that lie a considerable distance beyond Port Alberni, and when they come over that range of mountains they are apt to run into a foggy condition preventing them from going on. They circle around a bit; their only alternative is to go back to Vancouver, and they might possibly not have enough gas to go there, whereas if they had a landing stage in the vicinity of Port Alberni they could land there and wait a few hours, when the fog would lift and they could go on, or at any rate they could make a safe landing without any danger of crashing from fog or lack of gas.
An air base has been located in the vicinity, and I think I can say it would cost the government nothing because the site would be presented to them. It is a suitable site which would not be too costly to develop. Last fall the city tried, and I did my best on their behalf, to get the department over which the minister presides to put a landing base there as a war necessity, but we were turned down from the point of view of spending money out of the war vote; yet the opinion was expressed by the deputy minister that a landing strip in this area would be of much value.
It was stated that the war need is not sufficient to justify the expenditure that would be involved in carrying out the development at this time, and further that the matter is viewed now only from the point of view of military necessity. It is admitted, however, that it would be of some value even to those who are directing military affairs under present conditions, and I imagine what leads them to this conclusion is the condition I have outlined, where a military plane might come over the mountain and find itself unable either to go forward or to turn back.
I want to emphasize what I might call the present-day value of such an undertaking, even though they might not go to the extent of spending all the money that might be required at this time. The suggestion, therefore, is this. Will the department, either for its usefulness, or partly for its usefulness under wartime conditions, and partly for its usefulness in the future as a development base for the city of Port Alberni-and remember that fogs will always be there in the future and there will be the same necessity of having a safe landing place-give any consideration towards construction, and, if so, to what extent?

I wish, however, to make one or two observations with regard to the announcement that the minister made the other day, in which he gave us some light on the negotiations that have been carried on in respect of world airways in the post-war period.
I believe that the importance of his announcement has not been recognized in Canada as seriously as it should- have been. The significance of the announcement cannot be entirely grasped without a bit of diagnosis of the tendency of movements and events in this present day in this present world. The wheels of time grind slowly but, as the sage has said, they grind exceedingly well. What one generation may accomplish or fail to accomplish or destroy is left for a succeeding generation either to enjoy or to suffer. One generation after another passes on, each playing its part in the process of events leading either to the world's happiness and sweet content or to the ultimate destruction of civilization.
Governments that have been given power by the people have authority, but with that authority there comes a grave and great responsibility. In making these observations and criticisms I wish to lay down a premise which I believe to be a fact, namely, that the world is gradually moving on toward a world dictator; that the stage is gradually being set.
Over the process of time the props are gradually being placed upon the stage, and perhaps the time is not so far distant when the stage will welcome the entrance of a world dictator. I state now unequivocally that any move on the part of any government of any nation that plays into the hands of international authority or control is aiding and abetting a programme which sets the stage for that coming world dictator.
Let me make it clear that I have no objection to cooperation with other nations, or, as the hon. member for Lethbridge says, we have no objections to coordination with other nations. We have no objections to international cooperation and coordination. But to propose anything in the nature of international authority and international control is another matter altogether, and I, for one, am personally opposed, absolutely and positively, to any authority and control being passed over from the Canadian people to any outside body.
May I make a little analysis of the minister's speech of March 17? I find that on page 1577 of Hansard the minister is reported to have stated:
The briefest fashion in which I can describe the situation which will exist at the end of the war is that the position and sovereignty of the Canadian government have been protected completely in all arrangements that have been made'.
I do not know whether the minister made a little slip there or not; but I do wish to ask him when he thinks the Canadian government ever became sovereign. If he had talked about the sovereignty of the Canadian people that would have been another thing, but I maintain that particularly to-day there is a vast difference between the sovereignty of the Canadian people and the sovereignty of the Canadian government. I maintain that very little is done in this house by the present government that is in any way at all a reflection of the sovereign will of the Canadian people. I stated the other day that I doubted very much whether issues of this kind were ever brought before the entire Liberal party.
I do not want to take time further to emphasize statements I have made previously in this chamber, but I know what happens in regard to the provincial government of Alberta. The government there has a majority of the seats in the legislature; because of their particular electoral system they have a majority vote of the people reflected in that legislature, and when that government desires to introduce any piece of legislation that legislation is brought before a caucus of the entire party in order that the caucus may
War Appropriation-Transport

represent to the government what they believe to be the will of the citizens of that province, [f the caucus says, "No, this does not meet the wishes of our people," the government makes no further move. That is the procedure followed in a province, which is much smaller than this whole country; but when it comes to the larger and perhaps tremendously more important matters, what do we find the government of Canada doing? We find a handful of men attempting to impose their will upon the people of Canada without attempting in any way whatever to ascertain the will of the people. Therefore, I say that the government of Canada is not sovereign except as far as it reflects the sovereign will of the people, and who is to say whether or not this agreement as to international airways is what the people want? I am going to suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if the people realized all the implications involved in this international agreement certainly they would turn it down. Of course I am only a small fish in a big puddle; our group may cry with a still small voice, but I would say to my Conservative friends that in connection with ,a measure of this kind they are missing the [DOT]opportunity of a lifetime to place before the people of Canada the tremendous implications involved. I take it that a measure like this is the thin edge of the wedge to sell out to an international authority the sovereign rights of the British people.
Now let me go a little further; I shall return to that point later. I was analyzing the minister's speech, and at page 1577 of Hansard I .find these words:
We believe that in the field of international *air transport our interest lies in a liberal course of cooperation with other nations.
I have no objection to that if it means cooperation; but the thread of the minister's speech seems to go beyond international cooperation and to deal with international authority and control. On the same page I notice these words:
What is true of relations between the various parts of Canada is true also of relations between the nations of the world.
I wonder whom the minister thinks he is Tooling in making that statement. Does he mean to say that the relationship between certain parts of our own country-if you want to take the extreme, say the relationship between the province of Quebec and western Canada- is the same as the relationship between the Canadian people, as part of the British commonwealth, and the Japanese or the Germans or the Italians or the people of any of the South American countries? Certainly it is not. You cannot talk of the relationship between
IMr. Hansell.]
the people within a nation being the same as the relationship between nations; not at all, unless you are going to break down all international boundaries. If you do that, then I say you are doing the very thing with which I prefaced my remarks; that is, you are paving the way for a great world order under a great world dictatorship. Again on page 1577 of Hansard I find these words:
As I have already mentioned, on April 2 last year the Prime Minister gave a statement of the government's position with regard to international air transport, making it clear that our policy would be one of international cooperation and collaboration-
That is all right.
-and that we would support whatever policy seemed- best calculated to serve not only the immediate national interests of Canada, but our overriding interest in the establishment of an international order which will prevent the outbreak of another world war.
First, I should like to know who are the calculators. Are they the seventeen or eighteen men who constitute the government of Canada? Further, I want to ask what authority the minister has for being so bold as to say that such cooperation and collaboration in an international world order will prevent the outbreak of another world war. I say to this committee that it is a false philosophy to teach that a world order will prevent war. I venture the suggestion that under a world order, if war ever does break out it will be a world civil war. I do not say there should not be international cooperation; but the very moment we tie up our sovereign rights, or hand them over to any international authority with, shall I say, interlocking treaties bound up with that international authority, then when war breaks out between two smaller nations the world itself becomes plunged into blood.
I want to go a little farther with this analysis. The minister says at page 1578 of Hansard:
The decision which the united nations must make in the near future in the post-war organization of air transport thus is vital, and an enlightened settlement will go a long way toward establishing a lasting peace, and a new world order of security.
Once again he is presupposing something that is false, that a world order will bring security. A world order may and I believe will bring about world war.
He said again, on the same page:
From the point of view of practical politics the problem is to find some method of international control.
Once again he harps upon control. There cannot be any international control unless

War Appropriation-Transport
somebody gives some body international control, and if we give up our control to some international body then we are handing over to an outside power what is the sovereign right of our own people. That is my contention.
Again, at page 1579, he said:
Not only should some international air transport authority supervise the administration of the freedoms and rights suggested above, but the authority should also have power-
Note those words-authority, control, power. -to regulate international air services in order to prevent the dangers of unnecessary and uneconomic duplication.
Again, at page 1580, speaking of Lord Beaverbrook as chairman of the London conference of some time ago, he says:
Lord Beaverbrook added that it had been agreed that "the international air transport authority should be intimately associated with and responsible to any united nations security organization which might be established."
So that you see the plan ties us up with any united nations or international security organization. What we are doing here is simply tieing ur whole airway scheme up to an international authority which will have as its bodyguard some force in order to protect its interests in the international field. I say once again that it is a false philosophy to think that an international organization or authority can prevent world war.
Nor do I agree with the policy that is sometimes stated by leading diplomats that in the post-war order, peace must be secured by force. I believe that force is the absolute antithesis of the freedom of man. We all heard Mr. Anthony Eden, standing where you are sitting now, Mr. Chairman, addressing the members of the House of Commons and the Senate, when he distinctly declared that in the post-war world some international authority would have to use force in order to maintain peace. I say to you, Mr Chairman, that it is absolutely contrary to the freedom of mankind to use force. What we want is a world order where there is no need of force, and that can be obtained by a proper approach.
I have finished with my analysis of the minister's speech and I wish to refer briefly to the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in which he welcomes the government's move but, of course, is sorry it does not go farther. I do not need to comment on that, for I am sure I could not speak any more forcefully than the hon. member for Vegreville did this afternoon when he tried to show, and did show, the committee that the present government of Canada is indeed going socialist. I could not point that out better than the hon. member for Vegreville did, and
when he was trying to point out to the committee the danger of any policy that would' tend toward the disintegration of the British empire, the feeling came over me how strange it was that here was a man born in the Ukraine who came here with his family at two or three years of age and was brought up and educated in Canada, and now in his youth was standing here in the House of Commons and calling for the safeguarding of the sovereign rights of the Canadian people under British democracy, while all around us and by the minister's own policy we are attempting to take away some of the sovereign rights of our people and hand them over to some outside authority. Is the minister Canadian? Is the Prime Minister Canadian? For they are the ones who are responsible. Is the cabinet truly Canadian and British? I say that in this matter I will bet on the hon. member for Vegreville as being the truly British Canadian. The proof of the pudding is in the eating. I want a government in Canada that will safeguard the rights of our Canadian people.
I was going to refer to the statement made by the leader of the C.C.F. party who also welcomes the government's stand, but I shall refer to it only in this way. The leader of the C.C.F. party must really try to distinguish between cooperation and control. This is what he says at page 1656 of Hansard:
Accordingly in the field of international air transportation it becomes apparent and, I think, important, that only public control should function. International cooperation does not mean, in reality, a diminution of national sovereignty. What it really means is, sometimes, the transfer-
Mr. Martin: The expansion of it.
Mr. Coldwell: -of national sovereignty between nations.
He continues, but he does not get along very far before he uses the term "international control." We are in favour of international cooperation, but I for one am not in favour of any centralized international body controlling anything inside Canada.
In what I have to say now I do not intend to pose as an authority on constitutional matters. I might as well confess at the start that I do not know anything about them. Strange as it may seem, I am going to talk about something about which I do not know anything. That is just a simple confession; the rest of the members of the House of Commons have never confessed that as yet. I doubt very much whether a constitutional government has any right to sign an agreement or treaty of this kind. I have done a little browsing, some snatching here and some
War Appropriation-Transport

snatching there, in order to get a little information. I read the British North America Act, and the only thing I could find in it referring to foreign treaties or agreements was section 132, which reads:
The parliament and government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British empire, towards foreign countries arising under treaties between the empire and such foreign countries.
I tried to study what might be meant by treaties. Generally speaking, I think that would be confined to peace treaties and international trade agreements. I can quite understand the logic that nations must make agreements with other nations, but I doubt very' much whether any agreement that purports to hand over any of the sovereign or civil or other rights can be made by any government. Whether or not that would be constitutional, I do not know, but I doubt very much that it could be done. It certainly is not common sense. I should like to ask when the people of Canada gave the government power to hand over any of the sovereign rights of the people to any other country, much less to any international authority that would be responsible to no one.
In connection with treaties and so forth I also did a little browsing. I have before me a book entitled, "Methods of Ratification of Treaties," published by the government printing office at Washington. This covers the history of certain treaties. On page 11 reference is made to the treaty entered into at the close of the last war, and I quote as follows:
. Lloyd George made the following statement in the House of Commons, on February 11-
That would be 1919.
-in regard to treaty ratification:
The third question asked about the peace conference was whether the treaty will be placed upon the table of the house before ratification. I believe that is the ordinary course. Of course, subject to the ratification of the treaty, the representatives of this country will follow' the same course as the representatives of every other country and provisionally sign the treaty at the peace conference. The treaty will undoubtedly then be placed upon the table of the house for ratification. I believe constitutionally there are parts of the treaty which must be placed upon the table of the house by the constitution of this country. If the House of Commons chooses to repudiate the treaty the House of Commons is all powerful.
I know what the minister will say to that, namely', that that is exactly what we are doing

here. I have not made a study of what parts of the treaty Mr. Lloyd George was referring to when he said:
I believe constitutionally there are parts of the treaty which must be placed upon the table of the house by the constitution of this country.
There must have been something in there which he did not consider the government had a right to sign apart from the approval of the house. Reference is made on page 16 to what Mr. Gladstone said along the same line in days gone by. I have very little more to say except that I question the right of any government to sign over to any other authority anything that belongs to the people of Canada. I can understand a gift of money being made such as has been done in the past few sessions; I can understand a gift of materials, but I cannot understand how any government has the authority to hand over the rights of the people. It is very easy to hand over the sovereign rights of the people, but it will take a war to get those sovereign rights back again.
I conclude by saying what I started out to say, that the picture is gradually being filled in. I believe that in the world to-day there are two great forces at work. That applies not only to this country, but to the world in general. One force is attempting to bring about a world dictatorship under a certain type of world state socialism. On the other hand there are those who are struggling to maintain the freedom of man. I know that some one will accuse me of uttering platitudes, it will be said that I am talking in terms that are ethereal and so forth, but may I make the following quotation:
Some of the biggest men in the United States in the field of commerce and manufacturing are afraid of somebody, are afraid of some thing. They know there is a power somewhere, so organized, so subtle, so watchful, so interlocked, so complete, so pervasive that they had better not speak above their breath when they speak in condemnation of it.
That is a statement by the late President Wilson of the United States. I say that there are sinister forces which operate behind the scenes of human affairs and have for their objective the ultimate destruction of free agency among men, and this cannot be assigned to mere chance. I cail upon the members of the House of Commons to rise in defence of the freedom of our people. I know the minister will say that this does not interfere with their freedom, but I say it is dangerous in that it represents the thin edge of the wedge, in that it seeks to establish that a few men at the head of the government can hand over control to an international body.

We are not opposed to international agreements.
Mr. HOW'E: Well, what are we attempting to do in the Canadian proposal for regulation of international air transport? Prior to the war, in order to extend our air service, we will say to South America, it would be necessary for the government of Canada to enter into a treaty with every country which must be crossed en route. If one country objected, then unless it were possible to avoid that country by plotting a route around it, the service would be impossible. Air services are now established under that arrangement, but with extreme difficulty. Take, for example, the ease of Canada, which stands at the crossroads of all the important air routes of the northern hemisphere. We will say that Canada refuses to enter into any international agreement and that it will permit planes to fly over our territory only by agreement with each country concerned. What would be our position? Every country in North America and in Europe would be demanding from Canada a bilateral agreement. Suppose we gave it to one country and refused it to. another; would that lead to friendly relations, or would it lead to war? Suppose we refused permission for Russia to cross Canada with
War Appropriation-Transport

an air service to the United States, yet permitted the United States to cross Canada to fly to Russia, would that be a comfortable position for Canada? We believe that there is potential disagreement of a serious nature in such a system of carrying on international air transport by bilateral agreement. It is not impossible, but it certainly has presented in the past great difficulties, and will in the future present great or greater difficulties as the volume of international aviation steps up.
We believe that all countries can agree on certain freedoms. One is freedom of innocent passage; that is, the right of a plane of a peaceful country to fly over the territory of another peaceful country. We also believe that there should be the right to land to refuel in any country, by international agreement. on the same principle as the freedom of the sea. However, it is accepted, by those who know the technical difficulties of flying haphazard over another country, that there must be regulation of the exercise of the right of innocent passage and the right to land and refuel.
Canada has proposed certain other freedoms which can be exercised only by international regulations, namely, the right to pick up in another country passengers destined for the country of origin of the plane, and to take from such country of origin its own nationals destined for another country. These freedoms can be exercised only by international regulations. Therefore Canada proposes an international body to carry out the provisions of these four freedoms in the interests of international aviation as a whole.
The document submitted is Canada's proposal. It is by no means a treaty. We are not asking the house to ratify a treaty. We have advanced it as a proposal. from Canada for a basis of agreement with other nations interested in international aviation. It has been suggested, I believe, by the last speaker that Canada is doing this surreptitiously without the support of the majority party in this house and without the knowledge of all members of the house. I cannot imagine how that conclusion can be reached. Canada is the one country of the united nations that has placed its full air policy before the house and before the people of the country. We invite discussion on the policy and, when the time comes, if agreement can be reached, we will then follow the tradition of the British government. The government will take the responsibility for agreeing on the part of Canada and later will ask parliament to ratify Canada's signature to the agreement. That is British policy, which has been followed for a great many years. I think my hon. 
friend will find that the doubts he has expressed in that regard are unjustified. I do ask him to study the past history of international aviation and to read the agreement of 1919 to which Canada is a party and then to make up his mind whether further freedom under a convention is not in the best interest of post-war civil aviation.

On March 17 the Minister of Munitions and Supply made a statement to the house on the international discussions on air transport policy which took place in London in October last. He told the house that all the participants were desirous of improving the air services between their territories, and agreed that such development must take place within an international framework, and that closed discriminatory systems could only promote disharmony, and endanger the chances of reaching that broad agreement which is necessary.
The minister also tabled the draft international air transport convention which, by consent of the house, was published in Hansard of March 17, at page 1580. I would not be surprised, Mr. Chairman, if you thought it necessary that I should make the same confession that was made so humbly a minute ago by the hon. member for Macleod, namely, that I am going to speak about something I know nothing about. Strange as it may seem, one cannot be misled if one listens to the voice that is heard in one's subconscious being or the voice that comes through a very faithful kind of aerial, the voice that gives us warnings of dangers to be encountered. If we listen to this voice we cannot be misled, and it tells me that this project of international control for
air services in the post-war period does *obviously present some dangers to the autonomy of the country.
A careful examination of these agreements makes me believe that we are preparing another monster cartel which will take charge of all air lines of the world. We have had already for many years, and more specially in these last years, and again these last days, the occasion of complaining about monopolies and cartels; and lately we heard from reliable authority that if we are in the midst of the most terrible cataclysm ever known in the past, it is due to the work of those monopolies and cartels. At the present time, we are endeavouring to prepare a post-war policy and are studying all kinds of projects for social security and post-war reconstruction; but my contention is that if we do not go to the root of the sore, if we do not remove the real causes of the present conflict, if we allow these monopolies and cartels to survive and not only that, but if we encourage the formation of new monopolies and cartels, we shall be again facing, not an enduring peace that everybody desires, but only a temporary truce.
Without commenting for the moment on the opportunity of nationalizing our large enterprises, but favouring in all cases a direct and efficient control over these large enterprises, I think it must, without doubt, be admitted, with regard to air transport, that these Canadian air lines companies have been formed under Canadian laws and certainly have some recognized rights.
Enterprises like our railroad systems and air lines services are so huge that there can be no question of provincial or municipal control or of any cooperative ownership. Nevertheless the government would do the wrong thing to force them into an international cartel, and so much the better if they are willing to remain independent. These companies, having largely contributed to the easing of the transportation of war materials and members of armed forces as well as civilians, deserve a better reward for their admirable achievement.
I should like to mention also the help that was given to the development of the unknown sections of the country by companies like Trans-Canada Air Lines, Canadian Pacific Air Lines and many other smaller companies, which have all contributed, to a large extent, to geological surveys, to the development of our mining areas and to the exploitations of our hydraulic powers, and therefore to the development of all our natural resources.
Having always been opposed to all the cartels, I strongly objected to the amalgamation of our railway systems, because I believed that such an amalgamation would result in another
War Appropriation-Transport

monopoly which would become the supermaster of all our transportation systems; and unfortunately not to the benefit of the public. I wonder how, being opposed as the majority of our people are, to such an amalgamation, when it comes to air lines, which is another means of transportation, they could accept a project such as the one proposed in London last October. I am under the impression that the public would be very suspicious of this project, especially when it is brought up by a government that has lost the confidence of the people.
I wish to recall the fact that for the last two years the government has lost every byelection; and this, according to the Prime Minister's own word in this house in 1934, shows that this government is no longer the representative of the people of this country. Therefore, how can a government be entitled to adopt a policy that will bind the future of our country, especially with so vast a scheme as the one coming out of this London convention? Furthermore, this is much more important, when everybody knows that as soon as the government decides to hold a general election, it will be thrown out of power.
The public would be interested to know- and I wonder if the minister could not give the committee some information in this regard- who are the real sponsors, and who are the technical and financial advisers who led the political authorities to such an agreement. I wonder if we would not find among them some who are very closely connected with this famous Bank of International Settlement?
There is so much yet unknown in this project; it requires so many explanations. People are so worried about the future of the country, that they will ask themselves if we are still heading to the aim for which we are supposed to be fighting. The people would be so glad to be assured that our war targets are still the defence of civilization, the maintenance of our liberties and the safeguarding of property rights and so forth. With all that is going on to-day, wfith all these new schemes, they are asking themselves if they will not be once more misled, especially when they consider that the establishment of the post-war policy comes from a government that, as I said a few minutes ago, has no longer the confidence of the electorate. Would it not be only fair, logical and just to submit this future policy, which is such a drastic one, to the decision of the people, so that the democracy for which we are supposed to be fighting at the present time would not be a "vain mot?"
Furthermore, a project such as this one makes the people much more suspicious, when they know that within a short time there will

be in London an imperial conference, at which other like projects may be adopted, which will bind the future of our country. Our people would like to rely on Prime Minister Churchill's statement wdien he said that an imperial conference would take place in London at which all the dominions would be represented by newly elected prime ministers. There is only one way to correct all this, only one way to assure the people of the country that nothing will be done against their will, namely, the immediate holding of a general election. No one can conceive that a government, which is supposed to know what is going on in the country, would refrain from asking the people to confirm its mandate, and to renew it, so as to enable the government to make such important commitments.

speechtext:
I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Macleod and also to the address made by the hon. member for Vegre-ville, and I do not think the minister answered the thesis that they advanced. I agree with the minister that in so far as this discussion is concerned it is but an exploratory one for the purpose of ascertaining the views of the members of this committee, and that the convention is merely tentative. But I should like to have a statement from the minister this evening in regard to several matters, some of which I dealt with when I spoke on March 23. I asked a number of questions on that occasion, but the minister did not have an opportunity that evening to answer them. Unless we have an answer to a number of questions that were asked this afternoon and also earlier in this debate we are merely shadow-boxing with unrealities. We should know the position the government is taking, first in connection with the international set-up; second and very important, the attitude of the government toward a British empire or commonwealth air scheme operating under an international authority, and, finally, various matters in connection with the domestic field which as yet have not been explained.
I intend to ask a number of questions in order that we may get the picture as to what has taken place at the various conferences that have been held in recent weeks; something of the decisions made or the agreements reached at the Beaverbrook conference that took place in October, and the reasons that have caused the minister to change the opinion he expressed in the past, that railway companies were an ideal medium to operate airways in this country.
I was surprised at a statement made by the minister in reply to an hon. member who-

War Appropriation-Transport
referred to some contention that had been made by the Aeronautical Institute of Canada. The minister, if I took down his words correctly, said, "We would prefer that the Aeronautical Institute of Canada was not so active in regard to post-war aviation at this time." Why? The minister has enunciated the policy which the government is to put into effect one year after the cessation of hostilities. Why should the institute not be allowed and, indeed, invited to consider the propositions that have been put forward, and to make suggestions in order to ensure that the domestic policy to be put into operation in this country will be the very best available?
The hon. member for Macleod referred to an international authority, and the minister stated that there had been previous conventions, beginning with what was known as the Paris convention of 1919, and so on through the years. I ask the minister whether under the Paris convention any power was conferred upon an international authority similar to that contained in article VII of this convention, which provides:
If an air carrier licensed by the board or a regional council is of the opinion that the airports or other ground facilities on the territory of a member state are not reasonably adequate for the safe, regular, efficient and economical operation of the air services which it is permitted by its licence to perform, it may so inform the government or governments of which it is a national. . . . Each member state undertakes, at the earliest practicable moment, to give effect to the request of the board or regional council.
The next section deals with the matter of expenses. Is it not a fact that this article goes farther than any other convention designed to ensure proper, safe operation and the like? Does not this article in . fact grant to an international authority jurisdiction over the sovereignty of each of the member states, which heretofore has not been contemplated under any previous international air agreements? I ask him also whether the suggested international convention represents only the viewpoint of the government of Canada, or does it represent the consensus of nations with which there have been discussions? Has the U.S.S.R. been consulted as to its willingness to enter an international organization? I ask that question because 1 notice that provision is made for bilateral agreements between member states and adjoining, contiguous states. If that be so, the Soviet Union, having on its boundaries practically all the nations of the world, would not be required, in the operation of its airways, to enter an international organization unless it saw fit to do so.
Then the minister made reference to the doctrine of freedom of transit, which all accept
as necessary in the interests of post-war aviation, and which, as he pointed out, is somewhat analogous to the doctrine of freedom of the seas. Are the great nations of the world willing to accept the principle of freedom of transit? Have there been consultations; has there been any agreement in regard thereto? Furthermore, in an international set-up the position will be that T.C.A. will operate transoceanic aircraft. Does the government intend that T.C.A. shall operate a service round the world? If not, what portion of the world is it contemplated will be served by aircraft operated by T.C.A.? Without some knowledge of these matters any discussion of the question of international aviation is merely theoretical.
I now come to the next phase; this is something as to which I particularly wish to ascertain the position of affairs. I refer to the aviation position of the British empire or commonwealth. When the hon. member for Macleod mentioned the British commonwealth the minister rather forgot himself and departed from his usual dispassionate consideration of matters such as these to suggest that the Social Credit party was taking up the position of the official opposition.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Oh, no; I said, "the late Conservative party".

speechtext:
It was said with a sneer, and quite unnecessary in any serious discussion of this problem, and quite unjustified by anything that had been said. I am trying to discuss these matters without heat and without partisan considerations. When it comes to a consideration of the British empire and our relations within the empire, it seems passing strange that as yet the house and the country have been given no report, not even a cursory one, as to what occurred at the Beaverbrook conference. On October 18, 1943, in London, the minister vouchsafed an answer to newspaper correspondents who interviewed him:
The empire will enter future conferences on post-war civil aviation with a common viewpoint as a result of the recent imperial air talks here, Hon. C. D. Howe, Canadian munitions minister, said to-day.
To a press conference questioner who asked if this indicated a British delegate -would represent the whole empire, Mr. Howe replied "No." He said the dominions would have their own representatives. . . .
The minister reiterated previous declarations that the recent conference, to be followed by one with others of the united nations, was merely a clarifying "family discussion" on the background of the question and said only "broad principles" were discussed.
TFar Appropriation-Transport

la it true that a common viewpoint was arrived at in the conference which took place in London? Did the various parts of the empire agree that the proper solution of the empire situation was not to set up an empire scheme within an international set-up? I ask him also to say whether Canada's position was one of opposition to an empire scheme, and, if so, in taking such a position did Canada take it in opposition to the United Kingdom, New Zealand and Australia?
I read, too, a Washington dispatch of October 29, 1943, which quotes the New York Times in a Washington dispatch as saying:
. . . that the commonwealth air conference in London went as far as President Roosevelt in favouring freedom of the air. But Canada's position was said to have differed from England, New Zealand and Australia. The mother country and these two dominions share a 'ommon view.
Both of these analyses cannot be correct. The minister stated that we had a common viewpoint. I ask him, therefore, was the question considered at this conference of an empire set-up within the ambit of a great international organization, and, if so, did Canada's representatives agree or disagree with that -suggestion? I may have some further references to make with regard to the suggestion that I placed before parliament and the country on March 28 last, that we should set up an empire scheme without prejudice to the setting up at the same time of a great international organization to govern safety, after the minister has answered these questions, and to assure that after this war airways development and the development of aircraft will not spell the beginning of another world war.
To come now to the domestic field, much has been made of the fact that under the set-up suggested by the minister for the domestic field, our men who are overseas will be able to return to greater opportunities of employment than they would have under a scheme whereby there would be competition between the national lines and the lines of private companies operated by the railway companies. Doctor George Weir, speaking recently, said that he believed that after the war there was the possibility that 25,000 of our airmen might be able to secure employment in post-war domestic aviation.

Furthermore, the minister made a statement recently in which he said that a very, large number of applications had been made for domestic airline franchises in Canada, but that no franchises would be granted until after the war. The picture so far as the post-war situation is concerned is that Canada holds out the promise to the men who are serving in the air force that some twenty-five thousand may secure employment in aviation in Canada when the war is over. If we do not carry out that promise to the men we shall be doing them an injustice that is totally unjustifiable. I ask the minister how many are employed to-day in Canada in connection, first, with the T.C.A.; and second, how many are employed by private companies within Canada, and how many is it expected will be employed immediately after the war? These are matters

that must not be considered from a partisan point of view. They are matters for which we as members of parliament will remain responsible to the men when they return. It is they who want to know the answers to these questions. Our servicemen are not asking for charity. They are asking for the effectuation and the implementing of the promises that we make that there will be employment for them. Has the government considered both sides of the equation? Has it considered how many men returning from overseas could be employed should the present system of domestic air lines be continued, and how many more men could be employed if the proposed change is effected one year after the war? I ask the minister to explain these matters in detail, because all that we have had so far is a general statement. We have not had the evidence to support what the minister has said, nor have we been given the background which he alone can furnish to the house and the country.

I must say that I am not just clear as to what my hon. friend means by an empire set-up. There was a discussion of routes between empire countries. Routes between empire countries are wholly consistent with the principles which were laid down in the discussion of international aviation. But there are routes apart from empire routes. If the British empire were to confine its aviation to flying between British countries, that could hardly be called a comprehensive international system of aviation. I think the empire countries hope to have routes to countries outside the empire. Naturally an international pattern should be broad enough to include both.

My hon. friend was rather shocked by a provision that if airports in a member country were not suitable for international traffic other countries could provide funds to improve the airport and, if necessary, to do the work of providing an airport. May I point out that this is a voluntary association of nations; it is not imposed on any nation. A nation signs the agreement in order to obtain rights in other countries. Each country will have the use of airports in other countries, and I suggest that it is hardly fair to offer a country first-class airports in other parts of the world and not have that country offer in return first-class airports within its own boundaries. It is quite conceivable that certain countries will not be in a financial position to provide these airports at their own expense, but as members of a voluntary association there could be, I think, no possible objection to permitting other countries to do the work if the sovereign country is financially unable to meet the situation.
Perhaps my hon. friend will give me his next question.

Perhaps so. But there are other reasons. For example, I said in 1937 that the ticket-selling facilities of the railways would be very useful to the air lines. It took only a matter of a few short months to determine that the ticket agencies of the railways could not sell air transport successfully. A wholly different brand of salesmanship is required; and even though the ownership of Trans-Canada Air Lines was maintained by the railway, the ticket-selling facilities were completely divorced some years ago. There is very little in common between the two operations; they are quite different fields of activity, and I have come to the conclusion that they can best develop separately.
It has been suggested that the separation was an attempt to weaken private operation by forbidding consolidation into a great system. Private air transport in this country was developed as a series of small enterprises, and I believe that the development was more sound as a small enterprise group than it was as a unified enterprise. Unless the individual routes could be interconnected by another transcontinental system, I think there was ample evidence to show that the economy of operation was not as favourable under the larger system as it was under a series of separate operations.
The leader of the official opposition has had a great deal to say about small enterprise. I must say I agree with him, and I am shocked to find that he thinks there is no place in the air for small enterprise. I believe that the development of air transport as a series of small enterprises was a sound and healthy one.
It lacked certain safeguards which have since been provided. The weakness of the development was that as soon as a small enterprise became successful, another small enterprise would enter the same area, and if both were successful, still a third would enter, until the competition was overdone and one of the three had to go.

The policy of the government is to allocate areas to a separate air line, to protect each area against competition, and to give such assistance to the enterprise that it can grow into strong and healthy air enterprise capable of serving the needs of its particular locality.
I believe that is the sound method of development. It gives a place for small enterprise, and it allows returned men to enter the field of air transportation not as employees but as owners.

speechtext: In connection with the international set-up I asked the minister whether the united nations had been consulted . and, in particular, whether the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics had agreed to an international set-up, whether along the lines indicated in the convention or otherwise, and who the eight nations were that are referred to in the tentative agreement or covenant.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Let me make one thing clear. No nation has agreed with any other nation to do anything about post-war civil aviation. Can I make that clear? There have been certain conversations to obtain viewpoints, but nothing has been reduced to agreement. Not even the empire discussions have been reduced to agreement. There has been no ratification. None was asked and none given. My hon. friend asks how many nations have agreed; I do not think any nation has agreed with any other. He asked whether Soviet Russia had agreed. Certain delegates of Soviet Russia are on their way to North America to hold discussions of the type that have been referred to here to-day. I believe there was some delay on account of weather, and I am not sure whether the delegates have arrived on this side or not. They have an engagement to hold discussions in the United States and have been invited to hold discusions in Canada and in London, and other bilateral discussions of that kind are in the offing. It is hoped that, as the weeks go by, all the countries that are concerned will have had a chance to discuss the problem with other countries in an informal way, and it is also hoped that out of these informal discussions will come a basis for agreement. Final agreement can be reached only when all the countries interested sit down round a table for a formal conference.

speechtext:
I wish to make a few ' observations with respect to civil aviation. I shall not deal at any length with the international aspect of the situation except to say this: It might be well if we refreshed our memories with respect to the four freedoms of the Atlantic charter. As I recall them, they are, freedom from want, freedom from fear, freedom of worship and freedom of speech or freedom of expression. I think most hon. members will agree that if we go back at least to the years immediately preceding the great war and up to the present time we shall find that nationalism was rampant throughout almost the entire world. I believe one of the ideas contained in the four freedoms would be the replacing of nationalism with internationalism, and that being true, I think we should at least be prepared to support the internationalist idea in civil aviation in the post-war period.
With respect to civil aviation there is a local matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. During the period of preliminary investigations with regard to the aerodrome sites secured for the British commonwealth air training plan a number of sites were investigated in the riding of Victoria, Ontario. The city of Peterborough and the town of Lindsay, together having a population of well over 40,000, represent the two largest inland populated places between Ottawa and Toronto with the possible exception of the town of Pembroke, I think an aerodrome site located in that area would be on an almost direct route between Ottawa and Toronto. At least one or two sites in the vicinity of Lindsay warranted flight checking and quite extensive investigations.
I was pleased to note in the minister's remark this evening that he intimated in the post-war period consideration would be given to reenacting the principle of giving some assistance to municipal airport enterprises, and I should therefore like the area to which I have referred to be remembered when further consideration is given to civil aviation in the period immediately following the war.

speechtext:
I may say that we shall be
glad to keep the needs of Lindsay in mind. We should like to have an airport there. My hon. friend knows it is difficult country in which to locate an airport. We hope that after the war the combined wisdom of the area can find a suitable spot and that we can. have an airport there.

I should like to ask the minister a question with respect to the operation of air lines along the Mackenzie river valley. A gentleman from that country told me some days ago-he may not have the picture correct, and in what I am about to say I am repeating what he told me-that the airfields all the way down as far as Fort Norman are more or less under the control of United States groups. Are they wholly under the control of the United States army? Then, from the places I have mentioned down to Aklavik, under whose control are the airfields? By whom were they built? speechtext: Supposing I want to fly from Fort McMurray to Fort Providence, and then from Fort Providence to Fort Norman. Will I travel on a United States plane or on a C.P.A. plane; do I land on C.P.A. fields or do I land on fields under the control of United States officials?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: If you go at all you must go on C.P.A. planes, for any United States planes flying there do not carry tariff passengers. The fields in that area represent the ideal condition we are trying to bring about in international aviation, in that there is freedom of transit, freedom to land and refuel, and freedom to deliver passengers. You will have no trouble; if a field is there, you can land on it. As a matter of fact, my officer tells me that the field at Fort Providence has recently been taken over for Canadian operation. If my hon. friend lands at Fort Norman, however, at the moment it will be a United States operation.

speechtext:
On March 30 of this year the following question was passed as an order for return:
1.	Has J. Francois Leduc, consulting engineer and associates, whose offices are located at No. 354 St. Catherine street east, Montreal, obtained any contracts from the dominion government during the years 1939, 1940, 1941, 1942. 1943 and 1944?
2.	If so, for what total amount?
3.	What amount has been paid to them up to the present time by the government, and how much money ivas paid them during each of the above-mentioned years ?
The reply, as contained in sessional paper No. 263, was as follows: Contracts between the Department of Transport, air services branch, and F. J. Leduc and associates, covering the inspection of materials at various airports
under construction by the Department of Transport, were: Mont Joli, authorized contract, $12,877.80. amount paid $11,539.73; Saguenay, authorized contract, $19,000, amount paid $15,702.09; St. Honore, contract authorized, $12,000, amount paid, $11,968.36.
(Translation) Mr. Chairman, since we are discussing the appropriations of the Department of National Defence for Air, I wish to bring to the attention of the committee what is, to my mind, a downright abuse. A friend of the government who is a member in the Quebec legislative assembly has been awarded government contracts for $43,877.80 solely for the inspection of materials at three airports under construction. That member, Mr. Francois Leduc, has already been paid by the government $39,210.18 for the mere inspection of materials.
Why were the questions I asked in that connection passed as orders for returns? I would not believe that everything was arranged so that the government's answers might not appear in Hansard. That is far from my thought. But I want to know, down to the least detail, about the staggering price paid for the inspection made by Mr. Frangois Leduc, because I want and have a right to know, as a member of the Canadian parliament, where the people's money voted by this house is going. I wish to know whether the inspection of those materials was detailed or special or whether a general inspection was made.
Mr. Chairman, as civil aviation is becoming more and more important, we must provide immediately for the evolution of this system of transportation. All sections of our vast country should be the subject of a thorough survey. Civil aviation is destined to render priceless services in all fields: agriculture, commerce, industry, mail carrying, etc. It will become our most efficient protection against forest fires and other major calamities. Epidemics, which so often have decimated the populations far removed from large cities, will be tamed by the easy availability of adequate medicine, doctors and nurses. In other words, civil aviation will play a worthy part in the protection of our natural resources as well as our investments and man-power. I can visualize it in a still nobler role. It will furnish the quickest and most powerful help to future pioneers and missionaries. It will greatly facilitate the civilization of Canada and the spread of the gospel throughout the country. These last two accomplishments alone would be sufficient to deserve for civil aviation the best that our government can offer.
War Appropriation-Transport

It seems to me that the minister replied to the hon. member for Macleod in a disparaging way. I gathered that the impression the minister wished to leave with the members of the house, and, I suppose, with people outside the house, was that this scheme contemplates nothing further than what is connected with civil aviation. On March 17, when the minister introduced this scheme to the house he said, as reported at page 1577 of Hansard:
As I have already mentioned, on April 2 last year the Prime Minister gave a statement of the government's position with regard to international air transport, making it clear that our policy would be one of international cooperation and collaboration and that we would support whatever policy seemed best calculated to serve not only the immediate national interests of Canada, but our overriding interest in the establishment of an international order.
That seemed to me a horse of a totally different colour. This scheme is a great deal more than merely dealing with civil aviation. It contemplates an international order: in other words, a world government. I call the attention of the committee to another international scheme which this government is behind, namely a scheme for the international control of exchange and currency stabilization. Let me read this statement which I take from the Keynes scheme for world currency stabilisation :
(a)	The union might become a pivot of the future economic government of the world.
(b)	It might set up an account in favour of an international policing body.
(c)	It would provide excellent machinery for enforcing a financial blockade.
(d)	We have here a genuine organ of truly international government.
This is not the right time to say any more about that scheme, but we shall have plenty to say later. I should however, like to leave this thought with the committee, that there is a great deal more about this apparently innocent scheme of civil aviation than meets the eye.

speechtext: Will the minister kindly give me the details regarding the contracts which the department let for work at Saguenay, Mont Joli and St. Honore?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I desire to clarify, if I can, the real situation regarding Canada's position in post-war civil aviation. I believe that the members of this house and the people of Canada owe a deep debt of gratitude to the

minister and his government for the position he has taken on behalf of our country with reference to this problem. It will be recalled that he crossed the ocean in October for the special purpose of attending a conference with Lord Beaverbrook in London, and there met with the representatives of India, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa; and the nations of the commonwealth sat down and evolved in an exploratory way the attitude they felt they should take on this important subject. The minister placed on Hansard at page 1580, on March 17, the joint press release that followed that conference, and may I remind hon. members again of what was issued:
The- conference with the dominions and India on civil air transport, which has been meeting in London since Monday last, concluded its sessions this morning. The conversations were informal and exploratory, and the conclusions reached are subject to confirmation by the governments represented at the conference. Unanimous agreement was reached as to the recommendations which should be made regarding the lines on which civil aviation should be developed after the war, and as to the contribution which the governments of the commonwealth and empire could make towards international cooperation in this field.
Then, on the same page of Hansard, Lord Beaverbrook, in referring to the issues which they had discussed at the conference said that they were "adequate for testing immediate opinion in relation to civil aviation". That is as far as the commonwealth nations have gone. Canada, we are agreed, occupies probably first place strategically and geographically on the map of the globe with regard to post-war civil aviation. You must cross Canada going east, west, north, or south, in practically any direction. So that we are a pivotal country in whatever plan is ultimately agreed upon. I am sympathetic with the curiosity of hon. members, particularly those of the official opposition, who ask so many questions and endeavour to put the minister in a position where he might appear not to be taking the committee into his confidence as fully as he might with regard to the exact programme.
But let me point this out. The commonwealth nations have had their conference in an exploratory way. It yet remains, before any final agreement can be reached, to sit down with the United States, Russia and China. We are fourth in war production among the allied nations, and before the war we stood fourth or fifth in world trade. Yet it seems to me that, by the aggressive attitude our minister and government have taken, in the matter of civil aviation, Canada now occupies first position among the nations of

War Appropriation-Transport
the world because, instead of having a national isolationist attitude such as was taken by the great leader of the gentlemen of the official opposition a few years ago when he said he would blast a way for Canada into the markets of the world, this government has adopted the very opposite attitude. We have had the courage, and we have been the only nation in the world to have the courage, to lay before the parliament of our country Canada's full, all-out exact attitude with regard to international post-war civil aviation. That policy which we have been the first to announce it seems to me is a splendid declaration of international friendship and cooperation. We are now in a position to go with outstretched arms not only to the United Kingdom and the other nations of the commonwealth but to all the countries of the world and say: We have had the courage to tell you what we think should be the world basis for post-war civil aviation. Here is our plan. Now let us sit down with you as soon as conveniently possible and discuss it, and make changes where changes are necessary. But here is a basis for us all to gather around and discuss at the conference table, to bring about a final solution of this all-important problem. What more could one ask of any country? If the official opposition in congress charged the authorities of the United States with not naving placed before them a declaration of their all-out post-war civil aviation policy, there might be some point in their criticism. If some member of the mother of parliaments took the same position there might be some point in it, but as far as this country is concerned we stand first, the other nations in the world coming after, in the matter of friendly proposals for a final, definite authority and cooperation. This committee might well recognize that fact to-night. I wish to pay my personal tribute to the minister and his government for having had the courage to take a position of that kind and be the first to endeavour to bring a real and final policy into being among the nations of the world.
