This evening the minister told the committee that the industrial development bank which is to be set up would look after boys returning from overseas who might want to establish air lines. I find that the preamble of the industrial development bank bill states:
Whereas it is desirable to establish an industrial development bank to promote the economic welfare of Canada by increasing the effectiveness of monetary action through ensuring the availability of credit to industrial enterprises.
The interpretation of "industrial enterprise" is given as follows:
"Industrial enterprise" means a business in which the manufacture, processing or refrigeration of goods, wares and merchandise or the building of ships or vessels or the generating or distributing of electricity is carried on.
It does not say anything about aviation; in fact aviation would be entirely out. In the banking and commerce committee there was some discussion about a ceiling on loans, and the governor of the Bank of Canada said that there should not be a ceiling. Mention was made of men returning from overseas, and the governor of the Bank of Canada said that there was no reason why loans of $10,000 or $15,000 should not be made. However, no mention was made of aviation and, as I say, no mention is made of aviation in the industrial development bank bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Change the bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The bill will have to be changed. Evidently the minister was under the impression that the bank could take care of things of that kind. When the boys return from overseas many will be wanting to establish garage and repair shops along our tourist highways, and that is not covered.

speechtext: It should be.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

It should be, absolutely. When mention was made of loans of $5,000, $10,000 or $15,000 to permit boys returning from overseas establishing businesses, it was practically left out. We were talking of loans of $100,000, $200,000 or $300,000, and then we got down to $10,000 or $15,000 or $20,000. I think this bank should be able to take care of what has been mentioned to-night, namely, aviation enter* prises and garages which the boys returning from overseas will want to establish. There is every likelihood that our tourist trade will be greater than ever. The government is setting up a tourist committee, and a convention was held the other day to discuss these matters. I think everything possible should be done to encourage boys returning from overseas to set up garages along our tourist routes.
Mention was made to-night about Peterborough and Lindsay. We should have a field there. The deputy minister has stated that surveys have been made in the Peterborough district. That city is most anxious to have an airfield. It is one of the industrial centres of Canada. I think the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, (Mr. McNevin) stated that Peterborough and Lindsay had a population

of about 40,000. Peterborough and its suburbs have a population of about 32,000. The country there is rolling, but it is a beautiful country. Perhaps it may be hard to put in an airfield, but they have put them in in more difficult places. I think everything possible should be done along that line.
Mention has been made of the possibility of establishing small air lines, and I was wondering if the minister had in mind the selling of bombers and other types of planes. In a return that was brought down I notice that six Boeing planes were sold to the T.C.A., and one to the Maritime Central Airways Limited. Is it the intention of the government to sell these planes in order that, transport lines may be established for carrying freight and passengers?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The Boeings referred to by
my hon. friend were an old model of transport plane. They were suitable for transport work, if no better type was available, but they were outmoded. It would hardly be a kindness to anyone preparing to start up in the transporta-r tion business to sell him a bomber or military plane. If certain military planes are capable of being converted economically to transport planes, that conversion will be made, but very few military planes are. The intention is to make any reasonable use of military planes that can be made, but it is not to sell military planes just for the sake of selling a plane to someone to fly hither and yon. Unless they can be converted economically they will not be sold to air lines or to the general public.

The
disposal committee will be selling some of these planes after the war?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Some of them, yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
And
some of those planes will be suitable for carrying freight?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Possibly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In
the United States some planes have been turned over to passenger lines?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No. Certain military planes are capable of being used for freighting with a different fuselage, but such planes have not been turned over to the air lines. The Liberator is used as a bomber, while another version is used as a freighter. Both have the same wings and the same engines, but the fuselages ire different.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What use do the T.C.A. make of the Boeing machines?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
For carrying passengers and
freight, but the Boeing is a civilian model.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The conversion of our
aircraft from military to civilian use brings to mind one type of plane which the minister has not mentioned, the Lancaster. Can he give the committee any information as to the possibilities of using what Lancaster bombers may be still usable when the war is over, for cargo or passenger carrying purposes?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The Lancaster bomber is being used by Canada to transport mail and a few passengers across the Atlantic. It has not been converted for use as a passenger plane; at least it is not an economical civilian plane. It is a veiy useful plane; it carries a very large load of mail, larger than any other plane that crosses the Atlantic. But it will carry only a few passengers; it is not a plane which could possibly survive in competitive conditions after the war. However, as I mentioned the use of a civilian fuselage on the Liberator bomber, the same is possible with the Lancaster. The York was an attempt to put a commercial fuselage on a Lancaster assembly, but it has not proved to be the type of plane which is required on this continent. I believe a few have been built for use in Europe. We are hopeful that a fuselage will be developed which will produce a commercial plane that will be competitive. We are looking forward to that, but it will be a matter of a good many months before that can be brought about. That is the hope we have regarding use of Lancaster planes in the post-war period.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My understanding,
although perhaps the minister can enlighten the committee on this, is that the Lancaster is a much better machine from the point of view of transoceanic travel than the D.C. 4 would be. Would the minister give some information on that from a post-war point of view?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I do not understand what my hon. friend means by a "better" plane. Better for what? It is a better plane to drop bombs, but if you ask me to go in competition with a Lancaster plane to-day against a DC 4 plane across the north Atlantic, I can tell you at once that the Lancaster plane operator would starve to death. When we are talking about civilian planes, the earning power of the plane is the important factor. The DC 4 carries forty-two passengers across the Atlantic. The Lancaster will carry ten passengers. If it is a matter of freight, the Lancaster will carry a bigger load of freight than the DC 4 across the Atlantic; but, as my hon. friend knows, freight is not a pay load in peace time.

H. R. H. Princess Elizabeth

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: My hon. friend is, of course, speaking of the Lancaster as at present built, but he intimated a few moments ago that experimentation is proceeding so far as the fuselage is concerned, presumably with the object of increasing the passenger possibilities and to put it in competition with the DC 4 or another passenger plane.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes. That is one of a great many planes that are on the drafting board to-day as post-war possibilities. I do not think anyone can predict the performance of a plane on the drafting board. It takes anywhere from four to five years after a plane is first flown to make it a first-class aeroplane. I do not think anyone should speak with great certainty about what the Lancaster will be with a passenger fuselage. I think we shall have to wait and see.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I assume the situation at the moment is such that there is a possibility that the Lancaster may yet be the plane best adapted for passenger and freight use in the ' post-war years. As I understand it, there is no definite decision with respect to either the DC 4 or the Lancaster so far as post-war possibilities are concerned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We do know the DC 4; we can go and look at it. There is at the moment no such thing as a post-war Lancaster passenger plane. As I say, it is on the drafting board, just as are twenty other planes, for postwar use. Which will be the best plane of the lot, I am sure I cannot say. All I can guarantee to my hon. friend is that none of them will be flying within two years.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There is one matter on which I should like to get some information, having to do, I suppose, with the establishment of the new type of machinery designed to control aviation in this country. I will refer to what the minister said, as reported in Hansard, at page 1574.
It is proposed to establish a new board, to be called the air transport board, which will confine all its activities to air traffic, and which, in addition to performing the regulatory duties now lodged with the board of transport commissioners, will be charged with the responsibility for advising the government on ways and means of bringing about a rapid and well-planned expansion of transport by air. The proposed board will examine the needs for new commercial services, and make recommendations for their establishment and expansion, in both the domestic and international fields; receive applications for the services and issue commercial licences; establish tariffs and regulate rates; examine the ownership, financial structure, operations, and financial position of carriers, make recommendations for needed financial assistance; advise the government on matters affecting the operation of existing
aerodromes; report on the need for new aerodromes; and perform such other allied duties as may be determined.
Is that board to be merely an advisory board, or will it have mandatory powers such as are to-day possessed by the board of transport commissioners in so far as transport in general is concerned? If it is to have mandatory powers, then it will have to control all our international as well as domestic routes. If it is to have merely suggesting powers, then it is a body that in reality has no powers whatever; it is a pseudo-judicial body whose decisions may or may not be accepted by the government. Is the minister prepared to explain what he has in mind, and particularly whether the decisions of this new board are to be subject to the veto of the government?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The nature of the proposed board is quite different from that of the board of transport commissioners. The board of transport commissioners is a judicial board administering an act. The proposed air board is almost an exact parallel of the civil aeronautics authority of the United States. That board functions within the department of commerce and through executive powers of the president. The air transport board will be a board within the aeronautics branch of the Department of Transport and will get its power through the Minister of Transport. I think my hon. friend would not seriously propose that the government divorce itself entirely from air policy. That would be an abrogation of responsible government. The policy must be determined by the government, and administered with the advice of the air transport board.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, April 21, 1944
